Will the minister explain why it is necessary to increase the Mounted Police and distribute them all over the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that the vote proposed is not an increase on last year's vote. On the contrary, it is a decrease of that vote. But I am very glad to give my hon. friend information with reference to the position and work of the Force. The Act which was passed last year providing for the amalgamation of the Dominion Police and the Royal Northwest Mounted Police under the name of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has been brought into force by proclamation since last session. That Act provided that the headquarters of the force should he moved from Regina to Ottawa, and on the 1st February, this year, the headquarters staff took up its work in this city. On the same day the amalgamation was completed, so that from the 1st February we have had one federal police force discharging its duties from the Atlantic to the Pacific and from the international boundary to the Arctic circle.
The strength of the force at present is 74 officers and 1,734 other ranks, making a total of 1,808; that is inclusive of the Dominion Police who are now members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. My hon. friend has asked as to the duties of the force. In the first place, it is the only police force responsible for seeing that the law is truly administered and enforced in the Northwest Territories, in the Yukon Territory and in the Dominion National Parke. In addition the force discharges important duties for all branches of the Federal Government in seeing that laws are duly observed in which the Federal Government is particularly interested by reason off those laws relating to the public revenue or to the other matters which I shall mention in a moment or two. First, in reference to the Department of Justice. If any Federal Government property is stolen, if any cheques on Government funds are forged,-any crimes in which the Government of Canada is directly interested-the case is turned over by the Department of Justice to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for investigation and the bringing plf the criminals to trial. Then, the members of the force on the inter-

national boundary have co-operated in the past, and are still co-operating, with the Customs officials in preventing smuggling. They are also working with the Department of Inland Revenue. This branch of the work, I have to admit, has somewhat increased during the past year or two.
From what cause?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The growth of illicit stills in certain districts.
The outcome of my hon. friend's legislation.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows,
like every other intelligent man, that wherever we have legislation dealing with the importation and sale of liquor there is a natural tendency to seek to evade the law by the establishment of illicit stills.

Is the business of illicit
stills increasing of decreasing?
. Mr. ROWELL:	At the present time I
cannot give my hon. friend any information on that point,
It is at a standstill.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-but the Mounted Police are co-operating with the Department of Inland Revenue in preventing the violation of the law in connection with the establishment of illicit stills. They also co-operate with the Department of Indian Affairs in the enforcing of law on the Indian reserves, particularly the reserves in Western Canada. On almost every western reserve I think there is a detachment of the Mounted Police, and I am glad to say that the mere presence of members of the Force is in itself a guarantee that the law will be observed, for there is no class in the community which has a.higher respect for the Mounted Police than have the Indians of Western Canada. From the time the Mounted Police went into Western Canada the Indians learned that they could trust the Force to deal fairly with them, and that the laws would be honestly and impartially enforced as between the Indian and the white man. The presence of the Mounted Police, therefore, in connection with the Indian reserves is very valuable in Western -Canada.
The Mounted Police work with the Department of Immigration and Colonization on the international boundary during the past year of two has been of very considerable importance. Owing to the action taken in the United 'States with a view to deporting men whom they consider undesirable, there has been a natural tendency on the part of -many of these men to seek an asylum in Canada, and for the protection of Canada against the coming in of men who would not be desirable, the Immigration Department have the assistance of the Royal Canadian. Mounted Police. The Force assist the Department of the Secretary of State in connection with an important branch of its work. Where application is made by aliens for naturalization in Canada, particularly in certain sections of the country, the application is referred to the Mounted Police for investigation, and they report on the facts of the case to the Secretary of State so that he may have full and accurate information in connection with all such applications. More recently -and this is a little departure crom the general work that I have mentioned-the Department of Agriculture has asked the co-operation of the Mounted Police in enforcing the regulations which the department has recently adopted to prevent the spread of mange in Southern Alberta.
The foregoing will give the committee a general idea of the scope of the woTk of the Mounted Police in insisting upon the enforcement of federal laws. In addition to this, they constitute a reserve force available at the request of the provinces-and only at such request-to assist in the maintenance of law and order where the provincial authorities themselves are unequal to the task. Where the provincial authorities request co-operation and assistance for the preservation of law and order, the Mounted Police, as a federal force, is available to render that assistance. I think hon. members will agree that that assistance should be rendered 'by a police force rather than by the militia. I believe that in this-matter -that would be the general judgment of the people off Canada.
Mr. TWEBDIE-:	Have any cases arisen
where requests for such assistance have been made?
IMr. ROWELL:	Different cases have
arisen, the most important case, of course, being the occasion when, -at the request of the Attorney -General of Manitoba, accompanied by the request of the Mayor of Winnipeg, the Mounted Police took part in the suppression of the riot which occurred in Winnipeg last summer. From other provinces also requests have come for the assistance of the Mounted Police, but the cases have not been of grave public moment as was the case that I have just mentioned. This ibridf statement will give the committee an idea otf tlhe (work of the Mounted Police.
Mr. CAMPBELL.: Do the Mounted Police act in connection with the Criminal Code

in a province where there are provincial police?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. In any province in connection with any matter outside the federal laws to which I have made reference *they act only on the express request of the Attorney General of the province. In the absence of that request no action is taken by the Mounted Police. That is our understanding with all the provinces, because the provinces are responsible for the administration of criminal law. They should not be relieved from that .esponsi-bility, and there is no intention on the part of this Government to relieve them from it. Therefore, if there is, in a given province, any defect in the administration of the criminal law, that province alone is responsible for it.

If, in a place where
Mounted Police were stationed and there were no provincial police, an infraction of the Criminal Code took place, would the Mounted Police ignore the matter altogether?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In such a case it would be the duty of any ordinary civilian to assist in the detection of crime; to that extent it would be the duty of the Mounted Police officer to do so. But in respect to any offence such as my hon. friend has mentioned, no duty rests up the Mounted Police officer that does not rest equally on all other citizens in the particular community who have knowledge of the facts. I can quite conceive that my hon. friend might say: Well there is a policeman there; a crime has been committed; should he not undertake' the work of arrest? But if that were done you would at once come in conflict with the provincial authorities who are responsible; you would either interfere with their work or relieve them from a measure of their responsibility. So the principle I have indicated is not departed from in the administration of the law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When the
Mounted Police assist the provincial authorities on the request of the Attorney General of the province, is any proportion of the expense borne by the province, or is it met exclusively by the 'Dominion treasury?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So far, it has been met
exclusively by the Dominion treasury. There is very little increased expense in that respect, because the force is in existence; their pay and subsistence must continue whether they are assisting the pro-

vincial forces or not. The Federal Government, therefore, has not felt called upon ito demand compensation of the provinces in such cases.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In cases where the militia are called in to assist, the expenses are met, are they not, by the local or provincial authorities?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When members of the
militia, composed of men engaged in their ordinary occupations, are called out for such service they must be paid, and as that is a new charge upon the federal exchequer, the province that requests their assistance pays the costs. That is the general principle, as I understand it.
Mr. MACKENZIE. KING: Does my hon. friend not think that it might be advisable to adopt that principle, at least to a certain extent, with regard to this police force? It seems to me that unless that is done the provincial authorities may find it convern ient to use the police to the exclusion of their own forces whenever it suits their convenience.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If we discover any tendency of that kind I think it would be a wise thing to do, because Parliament would not be justified in relieving the provinces from the responsibility that properly rests upon them for the administration of law and the preservation of peace within their respective territories. We have not found, however, up to date, any serious difficulty in that respect; the demands that have been made for assistance are not numerous.

As I understand it, there seems to be fear of clashing jurisdiction as between the Ontario-we will say- or Quebec, police, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I think I heard the minister say that only upon the request of the Attorney General of a province would the Mounted Police act. Well, I can conceive of a situation where a crime has been committed ; the Mounted Police officer gets word of it, but he has no responsibility in the matter; he has no authority to act.
It would be his duty, I presume, to remain silent, quiet. If that be the case, because of the Mounted Policeman lacking in the right to be a preserver of the peace, knowing that his duty was not to interfere with provincial officers and being doubtful about trespassing beyond his duty, the crime goes unpunished probably on account of the time within which some police officer who has the duty, would learn of the crime. It seems to me, that, especially in the East,

where the Mounted Policemen are quartered, they would in many cases, be much more likely to be on the alert for criminal practices than some of our provincial police. If the full services which these men can render are to be taken advantage of, some arrangement should be made short of the Attorney General's request for their co-operation, so that the very fact that the Canadian Mounted Police are in our midst *would be an additional safety to the public against crime, providing there was an understanding with the provinces that they should accept the kind offices of the Mounted Police,-if you like to put it that way-and permit them to have carte blanche to pursue and arrest a criminal and to do the work a policeman would have to do in any well-organized community. I do not know how seriously the Canadian Mounted Police are involved in arduous duties; but many, I think, would like an opportunity to do a little more at times, rather than do a little less. I do not think any extra expense would be entailed if this Government were to approach the Provincial Governments with a suggestion that, while the Canadian Mounted Police are intended for Indian Affairs, forgery, as one federal crime, enforcement of law along the international boundary, and such like, still there are many crimes which do not fall within these categories and in which the Mounted Police would be very useful. It would be very proper for the Government to approach the Provincial Governments and say: We offer you the services of these men for the better order of the community; in that way probably showing to the country at large the excellent services-excellent, I believe, beyond those of the average provincial police-that these men could render to the country at large.

I have nothing but
words of commendation for the excellent services rendered by the Northwest Mounted Police since its creation in the Northwest. Subject to correction, however, I do not see why the Northwest Mounted Police was removed from the West do the East. It is true that, under ordinary circumstances, I would understand that anything which is dependent upon political control should be centralized at Ottawa; but the very name of the Northwest Mounted Police suggests that it is a body of men organized to maintain law and order in the far districts of the West. For over forty years, that body has rendered most valuable assistance, and the name and the uniform of the Mounted
Police meant that law and order were under their safeguard and protection. In fact, the name of the Northwest Mounted Police has reverberated beyond our Canadian shores, and any one who travels abroad hears quite frequently of the efficiency of that body. One has only to read the reports published from year to year by the Superintendent of the Mounted Police to know the valuable services rendered by that body in the past. Whenever I meet those fine young fellows walking with a jaunty air on the streets of Ottawa, I ask myself why they have been taken from the plains of the West where they represented law and order and sent to Ontario where we have a strong body of provincial police, in addition to having a strong body of provincial police in Quebec, and similar bodies in the other eastern provinces. During the period of the war, when the Government had some drastic legislation to carry out in connection with military service and such business, I could understand that the Government would strengthen the arm of the law for the carrying out of such policies, and I would not begrudge the help that might, under such circumstances, be given by the Northwest Mounted Police to the federal authorities. But now that war is over and all such troubles are past, I do not see why we maintain at such a high cost, this body of fine young fellows at Ottawa. Their place is in the vast solitudes of the West, on the prairies, where they can maintain, as they have done heretofore, British law and order.
It is a source of surprise for many people that, now that peace is restored, the Government should not reduce expenditure. My hon. friend might, perhaps, say: Well, we are threatened with strikes, if not with riots resulting from strikes. Thank Heaven, in the East at least, we have passed through the ordeal of the last two years quite well. We had no strikes of such magnitude as that which took place, for instance, in Winnipeg -and I have the highest regard for the citizens of that city who took the law into their own hands when the days of danger came. But in out great industrial centres in the East-Toronto, Hamilton, London, even Ottaiwa, Montreal, Quebec, Sydney, Halifax, jSt. John-where hae there been lany necessity for maintaining law and order with the *aid o'f the Northwest Mounted Police? Under former conditions, before the Mounted Police were called to Ottawa, they did then-duty splendidly, and the provincial police and the municipal police were sufficient to cope with any difficulties which might arise

in the East. Moreover, in case of a strike of great magnitude, or extensive rioting, the militia organization can always be relied on, and a municipality in which a strike or a riot takes place is responsible for the expenditure involved in calling out the militia organization. In view of the large expenditure that we necessarily have to face and the taxation measures imposed toy this House in order to meet our war liabilities, I would ask my ho>n. friend if in his judgment-and I am sincere in appealing to hie better judgment -we should not decrease the expenditure on the Northwest Mounted Police. In the East where we have law and order, where we have cherished traditions, and where we have no large 'bodies of foreigners who have to be kept in check at times because they ignore the law and perhaps import ideas which are not those of the East, the Northwest Mounted Police is not needed. Not that I disparage the efficiency of the corps or the high sense of duty of the men. I have paid enough compliments to the Northwest Mounted Police to justify me in saying that they .are more needed in the far West where they are more likely to come in contact with and guide the foreigners who have gone out there. Once more on toehalf of the taxpayers of Canada, I appeal to my hon. friend to reduce substantially this expenditure. I do- not know that the Royal Northwest Mounted Police is needed in the East, but they are needed in the West, and I would welcome their return to the West. The centralizing of the Northwest Mounted Police at Ottawa involves a large expenditure which in my judgment is unnecessary.

I nerver hear the Royal Northwest Mounted Police mentioned in this House but I feel that I ought to say something about them. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Maiisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) in two objections he has taken to the Northwest Mounted Police and their re-establishment. He Objects, first, on the ground of the expenditure involved. Let me say to him that I believe that the reestablishment of the Northwest Mounted Police on its present basis -was one of the most economical things this Government has ever done. No matter what we may think of the situation here in the East, we have to continue the Royal Northwest Mounted Police in order to police the Yukon. It is utterly impossible to do without them. We could, of course, increase the subsidy to the Yukon so as to enable them to employ a number of men as re-

inforcements, but that would be saddling an enormous expenditure on -a small population. Then there is the Athabasca country, which is now coming largely into population. There is already a stream of prospectors going into that oil country, and there is no question at all but what in a year or two the population of that territory will be substantially increased. We must maintain law and order there or abandon our attempt to uphold the traditions of the British Empire in this Dominion. It is therefore necessary for us to retain the Northwest Mounted Police. What does that mean? It means that headquarters will be at Ottawa as they always have been, because although iwe have had a headquarters at Regina, the city to which I am proud to belong, the Comptroller has always lived here, and Ottawa has been the real headquarters. So we must maintain the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and a department here with a headquarters staff, no matter hOw the force is disposed1, and that accounts for the, major portion of the cost which has to be incurred. Having that force, and that department, and that cost, what could be more economical than that this Government should unite the force with the Dominion Police and thereby avoid duplication? We have had the Dominion Police in Eastern Canada. You 'people in Eastern Canada are not so desperately good that you do not need a policeman once in a while. We know you do. The only difference is that i>n the East the policemen go around as plain clothes detectives, because the people down there are a great deal more cunning in their crimes. Our redcoat in the West is a great deal more respected than any Dominion policeman in plain clothes in the East. As we have to maintain the Northwest Mounted Police why mot combine the two forces and avoid duplicate expense, and have the one force perform all the duties which the President of the Privy Council has indicated, making it a Dominion- force, with the name of Royal Canadian Mounted Police? To me it seems a real step in the direction of economy which had to be taken, and I am very ^lad the Government has taken it.

I am going to ask the minister to re-comsider whether It is- well to extend the Mounted Police at least to the province of Nova Scotia. I have been magistrate, sometimes I have been called judge, of a town of between 9,000 and -10,000 people. We never had need of Mounted Police down there, and we have no- need of them

n<xw. I can remember distinctly sitting down one time and writing an .article for the press showing that from the 1st of January until the 8th of the following December there had never been one person in gaol in my town- of over 9,000 people.
I remember also stating in that article that I knew of 21 foreign languages that were spoken in that town.
There is no law against that.
Gaelic, too?

Yes, Gaelic and all the rest. Why do we want the Mounted Police down in our country? We do not want tbjm, and this House will be doing an injustice to Canada if they send them down there and pay them for nothing, for that is the way I regard lit. They are to. be sent down there, I am told, to watch .smugglers, to prevent them smuggling booze in from St. Pierre and Miquelon. I suppose there is not one single Royal Northwest Mounted policeman that ever saw a <sup!ful of salt water, and they are to be sent down, there to watch smugglers on the Atlantic seaboard. Childishness! I hope the minister will see the childishness of taking men from the plains of the West and sending them down to the breakers of the Atlantic. If you want Royal Northwest Mounted policemen down, there for that purpose, let us get them in Nova Scotia and train them. Do not send hayseeds from away across the plains down to Nova Scotia.
Order.

I have been orderly too
long. I have listened too long to that colony over there that has been charging us $15.75 a barrel for flour down in our country. Now, Sir, so far as the Northwest Mounted Police .are concerned, I am going to ask the minister to "forget it." I hope he will send none of them down into our part of the country for they will not conform to our police customs, and I say this as a magistrate of seventeen years' experience in a town of 10,000 people. I know whereof I speak.
What town?

Sydney Mines. I say that it is dangerous to send them there. I speak for 73,000 people in Cape Breton, and I can say that they will not appreciate any such intrusion. If the Government sends the Mounted Police down there those men will not only be unappreciated but they will be regarded as intruders, and trouble will ensue. I want to remind my hon. friend
from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and my hon. friend from Maistonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), who were both members of the last Government, that we had a big strike on the part of the coal miners in Glace Bay, a town of some 17,000 or 18,000 people, and in .addition there was what might almost be called a sympathetic strike in the city of Sydney, where there are some 25,000 or
26.000	people. At the same time there existed in Sydney Mines all the sympathy that could be evinced in a sympathetic strike. So that altogether there were over
50.000	people involved in the disturbance. Da hon. gentlemen opposite remember what happened? Do they .remember Mr. E. M. Macdonald-what at the time was member .for Pictou county-in connection with this affair? If hon. gentlemen do not remember this thing they can go into the library and Hansard will show them what Mr. iMac-donald said, and they will find reference to Mr. Plummer of the Dominion Iron and Steel 'Company. I see my hon. friend from Maisonneuve smile; he will remember that. These are things which it is well that the country should reoall from time to time. When all these matters are recalled my horn, friends opposite will think, and no doubt they will realize that the country is thinking.

It is a new experience to find same one getting up in the House and making the statement that the Royal Northwest Mounted Police are not needed in Canada. However, I think there is a good deal to be said in regard to the remarks made by my hon. friend, (Mr. Butts), and although I am .always glad to see that the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan)' always champions my old comrades of the Northwest Mounted Police, I cannot entirely endorse his remarks when he says that they iare the most economic force that has ever been organized for the maintenance of peace in any country. My hon. friend knows as wTell as I do that long ago, when their duties were more numerous and arduous than they are today, when they kept the peace and looked after the safety and welfare of the country, maintaining the observance of all the laws of the Criminal Code, there were far fewer men in the force than to-day and the expense was less than one-tenth of what we are asked to vote now. 1 can remember that up to the year 1914 their duties included the work that is now done provincially in the three western provinces as well as in the Yukon. They discharged their federal duties as well .as those duties

which are now discharged by the provincial police, and the work was done with about one-third fewer men and at one-tenth of the present cost. The question to-day is whether they are needed. We know' that so long as the Mounted Police are kept up in Canada under the present organization they will do their duty and do it well. But, as my hon. friend from (Maisonneuve has asked, is it necessary at this time to *add nearly $4,000,000 to the expense in connection with the maintenance of this organization while the duties of the men have been reduced by over one-half? That is an important question. Another thing about which not only I but, I think, all old members of the Mounted Police complain, is the fact that these men are now deputed to perform different duties from those which they should properly discharge, and instead of being maintained to enforce law and order, they are used as strikebreakers and put to other work which formerly they were never called upon to do. And .after the splendid record which they have made for themselves during the last forty years they are in great danger of losing caste and having the honour which they won by reason of long and meritorious service detracted from. I think it would have been a great deal better, when the Government decided to have a constabulary of this kind, had they disbanded the old Mounted Police and allowed them to retire with the credit they bad already established for themselves. The Government could then have organized a new force somewhat similar to the old one, so that there might be no danger, by reason of an amalgamation of veterans and new. men, that the record of the old Mounted Police might be in any way dimmed. I cannot see any use in retaining the old name, and there have been more harsh criticisms of the Mounted Police in the last two years than there were thirty-five or forty years ago. My hon. friend (Mr. Butts) says that he does not see any necessity for it, and I agree with him. If one-third of the number of men now in the Force could control the West and do the work of the provincial police, besides maintaining law and order and looking after the business of the Justice and other departments, I do not see the necessity for increasing the Force or removing it to the eastern part of the country, where, according to my hon. friend, it is not wanted. It is a great expense to the country and there is danger that the Force will perhaps lose some of the credit that it 
now -has all over this country for the good work that it has done in the past.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is one remark the hon, .gentleman has (made which I wish to deal with at once to prevent misapprehension. The hon. gentleman said that the Mounted Police had been used for strike work. That is not correct. The Mounted Police have not been used for strike work or as strike-breakers to my knowledge, which covers the last two and a half years, and I do not believe they were ever so used.
All I can say to the minister, then, is that they have been badly reported. I*t was, claimed that they broke the strike at Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am quite aware that
there are some who have made false statements in the press and on the platform in regard to the Mounted Police. I am glad my hon. friend has mentioned it because it gives me an opportunity of flatly contradicting the statement. They did not break the strike in Winnipeg. All they did was to suppress tbe riot and prevent most serious bloodshed and disturbance when called upon by the provincial police to do so.
They dispersed the mob.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They did disperse the mob.

That is
what I meant.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-and saved the situation in the city of Winnipeg. .Had it not been for the Mounted Police Force in the city of Vancouver during the troublesome months last year I do. not know that that city would have been as quiet and peaceable as it was during* that period. Our opinion is that the presence of the Mounted Police in Vancouver had a most beneficial effect, although they were not called upon to take any direct action in connection with the preservation of order. In addition to .what I have said of the work of the Mounted Police in Winnipeg, they did protect the post office officials who stayed at their posts discharging their duty when efforts were made to intimidate them and to prevent them from discharging their duty and carrying out their oath of fealty to this country. The Mounted Police afforded them protection at that time. The Mounted Police did not act as strike-breakers in any city.

Just one word in answer to my hon. friend from Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Butts). If we always had as good judges or even presiding magistrates as my hon. friend makes we probably would not need any police in any por-
9 p.m. t-ion of the country. But that would be too much to expect. The fact is that we have no more federal police in the province of Nova Scotia now than we had in the past. The Dominion Police, with headquarters at Ottawa, have always had police in Nova Scotia, and the amalgamated force still have police there. The police in Nova Scotia are in the city of Halifax, where the military magazines and naval stores are, and this Government protects that property by Dominion Police.

I do not rise to criticise in any way the items before the committee nor to criticise this Force. In fact, I am only too glad to' state that in m^ opinion the Government have done wisely in not only preserving but in extending the scope and influence of this magnificent body of police. I have watched them and their activities in Western Canada for the last twenty-five years, and I have no hesitancy in saying that there is no group of police officers which goes about its duty so coolly and so efficiently as does the Royal Northwest Mounted Police or the new force called the Royal Canadian Police. But I would remind the minister of the subject that I have brought to his attention, and the attention of the House on, I think, three different occasions, and that is the total inadequacy of the pensions to old members of the Force who retired some years ago and, indeed, in recent years. This veTy meagre pension, admitted by all, admitted in a former debate by the minister (Mr. Rowell) to be exceedingly small, has left a great many of these veterans in a hopeless and almost helpless position to-day. I mentioned this matter, as I have already said, in some detail on several occasions. I am going to remind the minister of the statement which he made on one occasion when I brought the question to the attention of the House, and I am going to claim from him now some effort to fulfil the assurance that he gave. I and other hon. members had spoken in regard to it, and on March 12 last the minister said:
I appreciate what the hon. member has said, and what other hon. members have said in support of his suggestion,-
That is regarding increased pensions to the veterans of the North West Mounted Police.
-and 1 am quite prepared to bring the matter to the attention of my colleagues and ask that it be further considered. Certain facts have been brought out this afternoon indicating conditions of greater hardship than had hitherto been presented to me in connection with this matter.
We have in this statement the admission of the minister that there was new information. new evidence of the need and fairness of this movement, and also the assurance that he would discuss it with his colleagues.
I took the opportunity, on two occasions or more since then, to bring the matter personally to the attention of the minister and to ask that he give it his attention and consideration. In addition to that there wai filed with the minister a petition or statement from the Northwest Mounted Police Veterans Association of 'Canada setting forth very clearly the hardships they were suffering and making a request for a very reasonable increase in their pension. I do not wish to go over all this ground again but I am going to again request the minister to give us, if possible, a definite assurance at this time that an increase in pension, which is expected and1 for which an assurance has already been given, may be granted in the near future.

I would like to add a few words to what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) with reference to the pensioners of the police force. I have been intimately in touch with these men for upwards of thirty years and I know that many of them, although they have borne the burden and heat of the day, have not had an opportunity of building up homes for themselves. To-day many of them have passed the stage in life where they can do very much work and the meagre pension which they are getting is insufficient to keep body and soul together. A number of these men are only getting fifty cents per day. Imagine a man trying to maintain himself on $15 a month in these days! At the time of the Northwest Rebellion these men did not get the land grant which was made to the military forces, and many of them think they were discriminated against in that respect. I do not wish to discuss the Force as it stands to-day further than to say that many people in the western provinces think that the old name should have been retained; but I db not- want to put myself on record in that respect; rather I am trying to secure something for these men whom I know to be deserving, and I heartily endorse what my hon. friend has said.

Is the
minister bringing in a special vote for pensions at some subsequent date, or are they included in this vote?
The pensions are included in this vote.

Then I might say a few
words in support of my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), who has taken the matter up on two or three previous occasions. Some years ago I communicated with the Government in connection with it, hut I never succeeded in accomplishing anything for the men concerned. Since the matter was brought before the .House some time ago 'by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre an exSergeant-Major of the Mounted Police called on me here for assistance. He had served twenty years in the Force, most of the time as a Sergeant-Major, and to-day he was trying to live on a pension of $18 a month. He was willing to fake any position, even that of door-keeper in this building, to supplement his pension and make enough to live on. Not only was he a member of the Northwest Mounted Police, .but he was also a veteran of the '85 Rebellion, and he also served as a transport driver in the South African war, rendering splendid service on all occasions, as his rank would denote; yet here is this man at 60 years of age trying to. live on $18 a month! His name is Desbarres, and he is at present employed by the Militia Department at Petawawa Camp, I believe, acting as telephone hoy or something of that sort. I think it is a shame that- a man who has given such good service to his country should in his old age be asked to live on such a mere pittance. That is only one case. I know of other men who have served just as faithfully, tout were not fortunate enough to reach the rank of Sergeant-Major, and they to-day are trying to live on $8 to $12 a month-men who have airived at the age of 60 or 70 years. We find those men all over the Territories. I know there are a good many of them in the constituency of my hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Knox), and I know there are some in my own riding. In spite of all our attempts in this House we have never been able to secure for these men a decent pension or a bonus. To-day we are giving pensions as high as $700 a year to our returned soldiers, and in many cases these veterans are just as helpless as our disabled soldiers. I hope that the minister will take this into consideration and see if it is not

possible either to increase the pensions of these men or give them such a bonus that they will be no longer objects of charity. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, at the time of the Northwest Rebellion, when all the militiamen received scrip, although some of them never left the East, the Mounted Police were not similarly rewarded. They complain,, and quite justly, that although they have been perhaps more highly praised than any other military organization in Canada, when it comes down to getting something tangible for their services, or even fair play, they have never succeeded in securing the .same treatment as has been accorded to others serving in similar capacities. When the matter was brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre on the Estimates last year, although it took the minister (Mr. Rowell) .some three hours to describe the glorious record o,f .the Force, it did not take him, I noticed, more than three minutes to assure the hon. member that his request for further assistance to the men could not possibly be met. It is mo wonder that these fine old veterans are tired of praise and have reached the conclusion that something that will keep them out of the poorhouse would be more to the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend in his
later remarks has evidently been drawing upon a very vivid imagination. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre has correctly stated what took place when he brought the matter up a year ago. He has been indefatigable in presenting it to my attention and to the attention of the Govern-_ ment on behalf of these veterans of the Mounted Police, and other hon. members have also helped. I have taken occasion since the matter came up before to look into the question further, and I have come to the conclusion that there has been no sufficient ground why the Mounted Police should not have been treated in the same way as the members of the regular forces who fought in the Northwest. Requests have also been presented to the Government such as my hon. friend from Victoria, Alta. (Mr. White) has just referred to, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) and other hon. members on both sides of the House have presented the matter to me very earnestly. I may say that within the past two, weeks I asked the Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to report on both these questions. I received his final report on Saturday, and

it is my intention to bring the whole matter before my colleagues when we come to consider the Supplementary Estimates for this session, to see if something cannot be done to remove what I think is an obvious hardship. I do not think I can say anything more than that to-night, because I have not yet had an opportunity of consulting my colleagues since I received the final report from the Commissioner.

While I have no
objection to an increase in the scale of pensions to ex-members of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, I have very serious objection to continuing this large force in Eastern Canada. In 1910 the pay of this force was $283,000, as compared with $2,355,000 today, and the increase in maintenance is in about the same proportions. We are spending to-day for this force over $4,000,000 more than we did ten years ago, and the force really has less to do now than it had then. The other morning I saw some ninety-five of these men, mounted, pass my house on Metcalfe street. They are a fine body of men, but it occurred to me that they could be more usefully employed planting potatoes than in riding around in red coats in Ot, tawa, Montreal, or any of our eastern cities. There is absolutely no need for them; no person has asked for them. The minister and the Government may have thought that they would need them when they brought down this Budget, but I think they can do very well without them. The minister should consider saving this $4,000,000 and let the Mounted Police go back to the work they were intended to do when they were organized, and the work they did do so well. Instead of hunting for worms, let them get back to the fishing that they are required to do. The minister tells that they are hunting for stills now. Well, that is not a proper occupation for these men; you can get other men for that work. The ordinary militia of Canada has largely increased over what it was in 1913-14; they are just as well able to look afteT the affairs of the country now as they were then. This wild rioting, and striking, and unrest, is more in the minds of the Ministry than it is in the minds of the people. All the people are clamouring for is an election which will enable them to. get rid of the Ministry; if they could get rid of the Ministry they would be glad to get rid of the Mounted Police; we need neither very badly. You are wasting $4,000,000 of the people's money, placing a burden of taxation upon them that is absolutely unnecessary. I had
hoped that instead of conning back with this item this year the minister would have decreased this force and demobilized it as fast as possible, retaining a sufficient number of men to carry cm the work that the Mounted Police were intended for and in which they were so useful. Instead the Government is burdening the taxpayer with the cost of having these men ride around our eastern cities as a show proposition for the President of the Council. I hope that this item will not pass.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In the Estimates for the Public Works Department there is an item of half a million dollars for Royal Canadian Mounted Police building. This item was held over the other evening because the Acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. J. D. Reid) was not familiar with the details. Perhaps my hon. friend would give us now some idea of what is intended in that expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not know that the item had stood over as my hon. friend states. Perhaps it would be better to take it up after we have finished with this one.
Was there not at one time an arrangement between the Dominion and the Western Provincial Governments whereby the expenses of this force were divided?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There was such an arrangement, which continued from the formation of the western provinces until 1916 when, owing to the conditions then prevailing in the West, it was considered desirable that the arrangement should be terminated and that the force, which at that time was considerably depleted because of the number of its members who had gone overseas, should devote its whole time to the work of the Federal Government. At that time, which was before the United States entered the war, the patrolling of the international boundary and the exercising of certain supervision over elements in the alien population in Western Canada were considered of such importance that the agreements were terminated. Thereafter the Mounted Police ceased to exercise general jurisdiction in criminal matters and the western provinces then took over the enforcement of the criminal law.

I can see where the Government have experienced a difficulty in this matter, with which I have a measure of sympathy. There is no logical reason- if we are simply to be logical-why this force should exist any longer; yet I should

i
hate to accept that as a conclusion, because, it is a magnificent force; it has played a splendid part in the history of Canada. I regretted even to see its name qualified in the recent legislation. So long as it was doing service in our unsettled country there was no question as to the need of its services or the value of them. But with the development of the country and the creation of the provinces a new condition arose, and I imagine that the Government found themselves faced with this problem:	Why should we maintain a
police force for Manitoba, Alberta, and Saskatchewan and not for New Brunswick and Nova Scotia? I imagine it is out of that difficulty that we have had that new legislation whereby the force is now amalgamated with the Dominion Police. I can even imagine that the Government have tried in some way to keep the force in existence, and in that connection I am sentimental enough to dislike the idea of its being demobilized. Yet, with the creation of the provinces and with the development of Municipal and Provincial Governments who have all the resources of civilization at their command there is no longer any need for the Mounted Police. The Yukon might need it, perhaps, but there is hardly room for a very large force out there, and in the Northwest Territories I suppose there is not enough population to require very much attention along that line. I wish that we could find some useful service for the Mounted Police. I recall an incident which illustrates the value of the work which they performed in the early days in Canada. On one occasion when I was in England I met a very distinguished Englishman who had just returned from Canada, and I was asking what had impressed him most during the course of his visit. After a moment's thought he said:	" Well, what impressed
me most was the manner in which British law and British justice had been stamped on that new country in the far West,"- and that was the work of the Northwest Mounted Police. I do hope that the Government can find some proper work for this force to do. I do not like to see them wasting their time around Eastern Canada because it is not the work they were intended for. Mr. iLEMIEUX:	I wish very briefly to
emphasize the points made by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's. I have the highest possible regard for the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and I would he very sorry indeed if the old members of that force were not looked after by the Government, but I have not been convinced by what the minister has stated this evening of the necessity of maintaining the corps in Eastern Canada at least. My genial friend from Regina (Mr. Cowan) is right when he states that in the far Atha-baska district and the Yukon there is urgent need for the presence of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. This only emphasizes what I stated earlier this evening, that the corps is not needed at all in Eastern Canada, but should be sent back to Western Canada in reduced numbers, and of course reducing the numbers would decrease materially the expenditure. I am not at all satisfied with the explanation given by the minister. He did not even promise Parliament that next year the expenditure would be decreased. We are asked to vote an item of over $4,000,000 under this head this year, without any assurance that the amount will-be materially decreased next year, although the people of this country are pressed so hard to-day by taxes and supertaxes in order to maintain our credit and meet the heavy financial commitments of the country. My hon. friend is not fair to the House. He does not justify this expenditure, at least as far as Eastern Canada is concerned. Four million dollars is a great deal of money. It could be applied, for instance, to the pension fund. Our soldiers are complaining bitterly that they have not received sufficient compensation from the Government for the services they rendered abroad. Their 
families are clamouring for an increase in the small pension which is being handed out to them. Every member of the House receives letters every day complaining of the small pensions, yet here we are asked to spend $4,000,000 and over, for practically no useful purpose as far as Eastern Canada is concerned. I repeat that in Western Canada, even in the organized provinces where the distances are so great, the presence of the corps is justified because law and order must be maintained at all costs, and of course, the force is also required in the unorganized districts. My hon. friend could cut this item in two if he were really imbued with the necessity of reducing expenditure, but the spirit does not move him. He asks us to pass this item of over $4,000,000 when there is such a crying need for reduction in expenditures, and he does not even state that next year he will materially decrease the amount. I am sorry the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is not here. We all listened with rapt attention to his speech in delivering the annual Budget to the House, in which he distinctly promised that in view of the large taxation Bill which he was imposing on the Canadian people the expenditure of the Government would be reduced to the lowest possible point. If he were here, I should like to ask him what he has to say about this expenditure of $4,000,000.

I should like to ask the
minister in charge of these Estimates how the force is distributed at the present time, the numbers in the different provinces, and the increase in the force that has taken place since 1012 up to the present time. I also wish to bear testimony to the excellent character of the force. There are thousands of people in Ganada who have a vivid recollection of the manner in which the force maintained law and order in the western provinces in the early days. It has a standing and a record that is equalled by no similar force in the world, and it is with no idea of disparaging the force that I am asking for this information.

'Mr. ROWELL: I am very glad to answer both questions, namely, that asked by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), and the question presented by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). At headquarters here in Ottawa there are ten officers and 55 of other ranks. That probably would not be greater, in fact, it is probably less, than the number at the headquarters at Regina plus the Dominion Police headquarters staff here and the staff of the Comptroller's office. There is no increase in the force in that respect. *So far as there is 'any change, it would (be a decrease. In the Yukon district there are three officers and 44 of other ranks. In 1912, the work of the force had not extended into British Columbia, and we had no men there at that time, but the work of the force has been extended to that province in the last couple of years. Alberta is divided into two districts. In Southern Alberta there are 10 officers and 293 of other ranks. In Northern Alberta, which extends right up to the Arctic ocean and includes all the posts up the Mackenzie river and two on the Arctic ocean-I may say in passing we have recently established a new post on the Arctic ocean at the mouth of the Copper Mine river, in the extreme north right at the heart of the continent-including all these we have in Northern Alberta 7 officers and 93 of other ranks. In Southern Saskatchewan, which includes Regina and the force there, we have 10 officers and 337 of other ranks.
In the Northern Saskatchewan district, which includes Prince Albert and the territory surrounding Hudson Bay we have 3 officers and 57 men. And it is not without interest to the House to know that we are about to establish a post at Port Burwell on the Hudson straits. Hon. members are no doubt aware that Canada claim's the Hudson Bay as territorial waters of the Dominion of Canada, and it is the intention of the Government to establish a post at the point I have mentioned where customs .revenues will be collected and sovereignty will be exercised in the name of the Government of Canada. In Manitoba, which, for the purposes of the administration of the police force, includes that portion of Western Ontario lying between Port Arthur and Winnipeg, we have 9 officers 204
and 239 men. In Western Ontario, that is to say Toronto and points west of Toronto, principally on the international boundary-Niagara Falls, Bridgeburg, Windsor, Sarnia, Sault Ste. Marie, Sudbury and Haileybury -we have 2 officers and 23 men. speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have no men outside of the city of Halifax. There are one or two /men who mky visit other parte of ithe province as occasion imay require. That gives the present distribution of the force throughout the different provinces.
I may say a further word in answer to my hon. friend from Maisonneuve, who says that there is no occasion for a force in Eastern Canada and that they should go back West. At least in recent years, and I presume ever since Confederation, we have had a federal police force known as the Dominion Police, of which Sir Percy Sherwood was for many years the efficient head; and when that force was amalgamated with the Mounted Police it was composed of about 182 men. We have always had a force in Eastern Canada, and there is no object in having two federal police forces with independent heads and all the expense incidental to a dual administration. No matter what the strength of the force may be, it is a matter of prudence and economy to have the federal police forces under one head with one administrative staff. While it is true that the official staff, the commissioner and his assistants, had their headquarters at Regina, the financial affairs of the force were always administered from Ottawa. The direction came from Ottawa, and, as my hon. friend from Regina has pointed out, the change is not so substantial in that respect as my hon. friend suggests. My hon. friend says that the duties of the force are not as great as in the past. Many of the duties which the force performed in the past are now being performed, it is true, by the provincial police forces, but there is a reason, which I think I made clear in my opening statement, why the force should be maintained at a substantial strength. In addition to the specific duties enumerated.



I mentioned the fact that the Mounted Police constitute a reserve force to come to the assistance of the province, if they so desire, for the preservation of law and order. The force was increased when the war was over by the return of men from overseas who belonged to it. It was also increased by recruiting, and the Government, for a reason which I shall state to the committee, takes full responsibility for that increase. The members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force who returned to Canada were exceedingly anxious to be demobilized at the earliest possible date. They desired to get to their homes in Canada, and the Government felt that it was its duty to permit their demobilization and allow these men to return to their families. The militia force of Canada had been disintegrated by the natural and inevitable operations of the war. Men had enlisted and gone overseas, and the militia units had been practically disbanded by reason of the complete disorganization. But one of the primary obligations resting on a government in a country such as this, extending from Atlantic to Pacific and embracing such a wide area, is always to have in existence a force, not very great but adequate to maintain law and order in the land in any emergency that might arise. That is the duty of the Government; and at a time when we had no effective militia, because the militia could not be reorganized at once, and when we had no effective permanent force, whose reorganization must be a matter of time, the Government believed that it was its duty to utilize the Mounted Police, with all its splendid traditions, by recruiting it up to the strength which Parliament had authorized, in order that we might have in Canada a force at the disposal of the Governments concerned for the preservation of law and order throughout the country. Now, I think that so soon as the militia is definitely reorganized and put upon a sound basis and the permanent force is put in shape, so that we may return to pre-war conditions, the strength of the Mounted Police can be decreased.
When?

Whenever the condition
I have stated comes about.
You doubled the militia.

speechtext:
Last year Parliament authorized an increase in the permanent 
force. The militia throughout Canada, I am sorry to say, has not been fully reorganized. It takes time to build up what has fallen to pieces as a result of the war, but we shall have it reorganized in time. Provision has been made to this end, but so far there has not been any extensive reorganization, and until that time comes it is the duty of the Government to maintain an efficient force such as the Mounted Police as a reserve available in case of emergency for the preservation of law and order. My hon. friend asks when the amount of the vote will be decreased. I have not promised a decrease for next year though I hope it may be possible to come down next year with a smaller estimate, but I cannot give any guarantee that I shall be able to do so, because I do not know that the conditions to which I have alluded will be so changed within the year as to warrant a smaller vote. Certainly I look forward to a reduction within two years at the outside, and I hope that next year we shall be able to reduce the vote for the Mounted Police.

One can understand that during the war there may have been reasons for voting special sums for police and for increasing the police force, but I think the country should be definitely informed by the minister whether the Government contemplates increasing this force or very considerably reducing it. My hon. friend said a moment ago that he hopes in another year to bring down a de creased Estimate. That is hardly sufficient, because we shall be asked when we come to the Estimates of the Department of Pub-

If the Government contemplates that this force will gradually be a diminishing body as the country gets more settled and each province looks after the maintenance of law and order within its 'borders, it is very questionable whether we should create a big establishment at Ottawa as a centre for the Dominion Police at the cost of the [DOT]amount of money which we are being asked to vote.
There is another figure to which I would like to draw the attention of the Government. In 1910-11 the total amount asked for the Department of Militia and Defence, chargeable to income, was $6,876,700. That was all that the country was paying for Militia and Defence. Now we are being asked to vote for Mounted Police $4,678,000, or over two-thirds of what in 1910-11 was required for the whole militia of Canada. It looks as if the Government were trying to make a standing army out of this police force, only calling it police instead of militia or an army. It is under the direction of the Ministry, the Administration can use it in any way they like and send it here, there and everywhere as it suits the policy of the Government. This looks like a far-reaching addition to the public expenditure at a time when we ought to be economizing.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman the difference in the cost of all commodities at the date which he has mentioned as compared with the preseent time. At the time referred to by the leader of the Opposition the pay of the men was sixty cents a day; to-day a constable's pay is $2 a day. Will the hon. member say that the pay of the members of the force is too high. The cost of a constable's clothing, his preliminary outfit was $54 then; to-day it is $150. At that time the cost of the rations of the individual constable was 22 cents per day; to-day it is from 71 to 75 cents per day. At that time hay was bought for $7 or $8 per ton; this past year we have had to pay as high as $50 a ton, and the average was approximately $30 per ton last year. This enormous increase in the cost of everything accounts for the increased cost, of the administration of the force, and it applies to the increased number of the force. My hon. friend has said that I should give 204i
some more definite assurance to the committee as to reducing the strength of the force. I have explained that one reason for bringing the force up to the present authorized strength, or for greatly increasing its original authorized strength was that, pending the return to more normal conditions when we should have a real militia force in Canada the Government did feel it essential to have a force in Canada which would be available for the preservation of law and order. We will come to the day when the force will be reduced. There is no intention of keeping the force permanently up to the high figures authorized last year. The force will be brought back to more moderate dimensions so soon as the conditions that I have referred to have again become normal. With reference to the future of the force, here is the question with which we are faced. It is 10 p.m. essential to maintain a police force for certain purposes. It is essential to maintain it for the Yukon and Northwest Territories. It is necessary to have a federal police for certain important purposes that the federal police have served during all these years. In addition we must have some force as a reserve for the maintenance of law and order. We can choose between having a permanent military force of a certain strength which the Government might consider adequate to our needs in Canada, or of preserving this force at a substantial strength. I do not think any member of the House will say that we should have no force in Canada. We must have some force. The question is whether it is wiser to have a military force of a greater strength or to have a smaller military force and keep up the Mounted Police for the purposes of a reserve force as well as for performing the necessary police duties. My own personal view is that it is better to have a larger Mounted Police force and a smaller military force than we otherwise would require. Hon. members may not agree with that but that is my view and that is the view that the Government has acted upon. Another Government might reach a different conclusion. It might consider it desirable to make this force a part of the permanent military force. We did at one time discuss that proposal but we came to the conclusion that the Mounted Police is a better force for preserving law and order than either the militia or the permanent force. With the splendid prestige they have the fact that they are in a community-the very fact that they are there-tends to preserve law and order

without thfir being called upon to exercise their functions as policemen.

The minister gives us his

The hon. minister (Mr. Rowell) says that in addition to the reason that the militia is disorganized, we must also provide assistance for the civil authorities when necessary. The hon. gentleman is aware that when any disturbance occurs the civil authority can call out any regiment of the active militia, and he is also aware that the civil -authority can call upon the permanent force to come to their assistance. Therefore, I completely fail to see what was the necessity of stationing in [DOT]Ottawa this detachment of the Mounted Police, and in addition building headquarters for the force at an expenditure of over $500,000. It seems to me that at this period of retrenchment and economy the -action of the ministry is in absolute contradiction of the statements made by the Minister of Finance. In the old provinces the matter of police has been left to the provincial authorities, it being one of the duties of Provincial Governments to maintain law and order and to have a provincial police force fox that purpose. I do not believe that the unrest which the hon. member described to the House has been manifested either in the Maritime Provinces, in Quebec, or in Ontario.
Except in by elections.

Maybe; but even in by-elections I think if only legal and proper methods were adopted there would be no necessity of organizing such a corps. Under normal conditions no federal mounted police force is necessary to maintain law and order in the older provinces; -and I think the minister completely failed to establish to the satisfaction otf this House that there is any urgent necessity for the organization of this force either in this city or in any other part of Ontario, or in the province of Quebec, or in the Maritime Provinces. The first retrenchment we could make would be that otf saving the $500,000 which is now -asked for a building for the Mounted Police in Ottawa. It would be easy also to economize at least -a million dollars in the reduction of the force to the extent of all officers and men now in service in Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime Provinces. I for one will oppose the expenditure of $500,000 for a headquarters building in Ottawa and such amount as is asked for to maintain the force in the old provinces.

My hon. friend is now askin-g for $4,674,066, whereas the expenditure during 1919, according to the public accounts, was only $719,142.73. I want to place myself on record as being opposed! to this very large increase. It is unjustifiable; so far as we can judge from the sentiment of hon.' members, no one wants this police in Eastern Canada. My hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Butts), who represents the most populous district in Eastern Nova Scotia, has put himself on record against the police operating in that province. The minister tells us there are twenty-one of these officers and men in Halifax. These men are not required in Halifax, and I think that is the sentiment in all the Maritime Provinces as well as in Ontario and Quebec. These police officers and men are forced on the people by the Government at a time when money is hard to get; taxes are being levied on the people to- meet an expenditure which is absolutely unnecessary. My hon. friend has repeated over and over again that these policemen are required for the purposes of law and order. But as I understand the constitution of this country it is the duty of the provinces, not of the Federal Government, to preserve law and order in the provinces. The Federal Government are assuming a duty that they do not require to assume; that the provinces are not asking them-to assume; that the provinces themselves .are well able to take care of. My hon. friend has said also that the cost of

maintaining the police has increased enormously dhring the last few years; that sixty cents was the daily pay of a policeman some years ago, and that the amount is now two dollars. Well, that is one reason why the force should not be increased. Why pay two dollars a day for policemen and all the expense of their maintenance if they are not needted? I repeat that this force is not required in Eastern Canada, and in all that the minister has told us tonight he has not justified the expenditure so far as that part of the country is concerned.

The hon. member (Mr. Sinclair, Guysborough), and the hon. member who preceded him (Mr. Vien) made it quite clear, as the fact is, that the maintenance of law and order is a duty resting upon the Provincial Governments. But aid to the civil power is a responsibility which is laid upon the Federal Government, that aid taking the shape of the furnishing of armed forces of some sort. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said that in the event of internal disturbances of any kind it'would be the duty of the civil power to call upon the active militia or the permanent militia to render that aid which the civil power is entitled to expect from the Federal Government. Well, the war has resulted in complete disorganization of the active militia. The active militia was in due course drafted into the expeditionary force; the expeditionary force has been disbanded; there is no active militia in Canada to-day. There is not an organized unit in the active militia of more than one hundred men. There are not one hundred organized men in Ottawa to-day. The Federal Government, therefore, could not, if it had to depend on the active militia, respond to a claim for aid to the civil power. And notwithstanding the increase which has been authorized, the permanent militia is no stronger to-day than it was before the war. The responsibility is upon the Federal Government to respond with a force of some sort. It chooses to take this particular measure in order to he ready to respond to the demand which it is legally liable to respond to; hence this proposal.

Does not my hon. friend think that all the unrest in Canada has passed away and that we are now living under normal conditions? My hon. friend is a gallant soldier; he knows that many returned soldiers are anxious to get. from the Government a better pension. I have letters in my pocket even now, one received 
this evening from a gentleman who rendered most valuable service during the war. I will read one sentence from that letter to show that there are crying needs elsewhere to which the money of this country could be applied rather than to the maintenance of a force which, honourable though it may be, traditional though it may be, is not needed, at least in this section of the country. Many members have received letters worded like this:
Dear Mr. Lemiecx :
The call was given; our services sought, we answered and gave up everything; have suffered everything,-yes, sacrified our all, and now we have been left to suffer the tortures of hell through physical and financial exhaustion.
I shall not give the name, Mr. Chairman, but every member receives letters of this kind every day from returned soldiers, returned officers, from widows, from orphans.
Now, $4,000,000, or even $2,000,000, would go a long way towards helping those poor people who, as my correspondent says, have given their all for the flag, the King and the Empire. Yet, we are giving a picayune allowance to those returned soldiers and to the widows and orphans, and we are spending $4,000,000, for which my hon. friend cannot give a reasonable explanation and for the reduction of which expenditure he does not make any formal promise. We are called upon by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) to exert our best efforts to incite the Canadian taxpayers to accept the last Budget with the best possible grace. He promises the Canadian people that he will survey the various items of expenditure and that every item will be subjected to the most carelful pruning. Yet, iwith a little waving of the flag, my hon. friend tells the committee: We have to maintain law and order until normal conditions prevail. With all due respect to my hon. friend, I maintain that the period of unrest has passed and that Canada is living under normal conditions. In fact, this country is doing far better in that respect than most of the other countries which have passed through the -war. Really, it is most discouraging to stand by the Budget and by the Minister of Finance, in inviting the Canadian people to accept the heavy taxation Bills, and on the other hand to have another minister of the Crown spending, without any good cause, $4,000,000 for a useless force in Eastern Canada.

What is the average cost
per man for the maintenance of the Mounted Police?

speechtext: Between $1,700 and

Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime Provinces?
