speechtext:
That is all included in
the statement which I have already given and put on Hansard, and my hon. friend can see it there. My hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair, Guys'borough) asks:	Why is the
amount so much higher than the expenditure for the year 1918-19? During the year 1918-19, approximately 1,000 of our Mounted Police were serving in the war, and the strength of the Force in Canada was reduced to its lowest point in recent years. I think it got down to about 300. The men who were serving overseas were paid as soldiers out of the moneys provided to pay our forces at the front, and, therefore, we did not have to provide the amount in this Estimate. The fact is that we are providing in this Estimate for a force at least four or five times as strong as the force that was maintained in Canada in 1918-19 out of this appropriation, not the total force, because so many men were overseas. The additional amount is due to the increased cost, higher pay and increased cost of subsistence since then. My hon. friend (Mr. Vien) states that I did not accurately represent the situation. I know the facts and I accurately represented them to the committee. The Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) have told my hon. friend about the strength of the permanent force, and the former Minister of Militia (Mr. Mewburn) if he were in the House, would confirm the statement. While he took authority to increase the permanent force, if necessary, to 10,000, he believed it was in the national interest to bring the Mounted Police Force up to a reasonable strength rather than to in-[DOT] crease the permanent force as much as he was authorized to increase it. It was part of his recommendation that this force should be increased up to the strength authorized rather than that he should bring the permanent force to a much higher strength. He thought it was more in the interest of the country to have the police force strong than to have such a large permanent force.

I was much interested to see the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) take the place of tire hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) when the latter sat down, but I should like
to hear what the minister has to say in reply to the hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend had been in the Chamber, he would have heard my reply. It is hardly right, as each new member comes into the Chamber, that I should be asked to repeat an explanation which has already been given more than once. We are anxious to get through with the business of the House.
Question.

Some hon. members are calling "question." Will they be good enough to be a little patient until we are through with this? The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Griesbach) informed the committee that the militia had been disorganized and that it was very necessary to increase the strength of the Mounted Police so as to ensure the necessary help for the civil authorities in case a disturbance should occur. I might answer my hon. friend by stating that no disturbance has arisen since the war ceased, and it is almost an insult to the peaceful and law-abiding population of the older provinces to claim that there is .a great unrest and that, unless this constabulary force is maintained and increased in strength, some uprising will occur which will imperil law and order and peace in our country. Moreover, supposing a local disturbance should occur, the permanent force of Canada, which is at present, if we take the figures given by the Minister of the Interior, over 3,000 in strength is more than enough to maintain law and order in the older provinces of this Dominion. If we take the figures given by the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), if a Mounted Policeman costs to this country in round figures $1,800 per annum, the 300 men or more who are maintained in Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime Provinces, would cost this country $540,000 per annum. It would be good economy to cut this $540,000 item from the Estimates submitted to the committee as well :as the $500,000 item which is asked in order to build headquarters for this police force at Ottawa. I would, therefore, suggest to the minister that he reduce the strength right away by the number which is maintained in the older provinces and that he should also do away with the item of $540,000 which is asked for the building otf headquarters in Ottawa, thereby saving the country over $1,040,000 which could be applied elsewhere towards the reduction of our debt.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Buildings, J'oO'O.O'dO.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This item is in respect of buildings at Vancouver, and Ottawa. We have purchased a property in the city of Vancouver on Shaughnessy Heights, where the police are now stationed. There were not sufficient buildings on the ground for the full accommodation of the police and their horses, and we have to make provision for the erection of quarters for the officers and for the necessary stables. The estimated expenditure for the completion of the buildings at Vancouver is $98,000.
Have tenders been invited?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The matter is in the
hands of the Public Works Department. They are proceeding in the usual way, but whether they have actually called for tenders or not I cannot say. The balance of the expenditure is for the quarters here in Ottawa. It will involve the erection of the necessary barracks for the men, an administration building, quarters for the officers and non-commissioned officers, and stables.

Where are the men
quartered at present?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At Howiek Hall. The
balance or $400,000 is not an estimate of the exact cost of the Ottawa buildings because at the time we did not have a site available on which to erect the buildings, and therefore it was not possible for the Public Works Department to give us a detailed estimate of what the cost would be. Therefore, so far as the Ottawa buildings are concerned, it is a lump sum estimated at approximately $400,000. One naturally cannot say what the final expenditure will be until the places for the buildings have been finally settled upon and tenders called for, but that was the general estimate formed at the time as the probable cost of the buildings.
Therefore it is the intention of the Government to maintain permanently in Ottawa 225 mounted police?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is the intention of the Government to maintain a force here in Ottawa. Let me say that the Government has always had a force of federal police here. These they do not require to pro, vide barracks for; they have not done so in the past. Every government of this country has had a federal police force in Ottawa. When my hon. friends talk about not having a Dominion police force in Eastern Canada they are going directly contrary to [Mr. Vien. 1
the whole history and policy of governments in this country. Is there any government in the world that has not a police force of its own? This Government has always had a police force at Ottawa, under Sir Percy Sherwood of late years. It is the Government's intention for the time being to maintain here a force of approximately 160 mounted police. The figures I gave to which my hon. friend referred included the old Dominion police and the new men who have come in.
How many mounted policemen are there in Ottawa at present?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There are 160 men and 5 officers. That is the strength of the force at Howiek Hall.
. Mr. VIEN: Which was not maintained in Ottawa before?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Which was not maintained in Ottawa before. It is not the intention of the Government to maintain a portion of the permanent military force here. At least that is the present view. If the Government should ultimately decide not to have a squadron of the Mounted Police here, the buildings erected would be suitable for any portion of the Permanent Military Force that should be stationed here. The view of the Government is that there should be a company at least of the permanent military force or the Mounted Police here at the capital city. I do not know of any government that has not some force under the control of the federal authorities in proximity to the capital city. That is the reason why the Government decided on the erection of suitable accommodation for a force of 160 men.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has any site been obtained'?
Are the officers' and the married men's quarters at Regina still occupied?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Regina is the training depot for Western Canada and there is a squadron at Regina with its officers. My information is that the officers' quarters there are occupied by the officers.
As to a site at Ottawa, there is a site which I think the Government can probably secure from the Canadian National Railways. That would not involve the purchase of property from private individuals. It is on the Rideau River past the Isolation Hospital.
Is the purchase price included in the $400,000?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. At the time that figure was put in, it was considered we would probably be able to get suitable Government property on which to erect the buildings.	.
When was the site at Shaugh-nessy Heights, Vancouver, purchased?
The arrangement was made in November of last year, and the transaction was closed in the early part of the present year.
What was the price paid?
It was $135,000 for fifteen acres of land with the buildings upon them, which accommodate 200 men.

This is really an item that belongs to the Public Works Department and it can only be voted in connection with these other items under the head of "Generally."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
This request of the Government is just another evidence of the delay which Parliament has had to endure in consequence of the ministry not having its business in shape so that we
could meet earlier in the year and make progress. Rather strong exception was taken on this side when the Government asked somewhat earlier in the year for a sixth of the Estimates to be voted before Parliament had an opportunity of discussing the Estimates themselves. I think that 'the same exception might equally well be taken at the present time to granting any further advance to the Government, but I gather that if this amount were not advanced at this time it would only have the effect of considerably inconveniencing the Civil Service, not only the inside service but the service in different parts of the country. I presume that hon. members on this side of the House will acquiesce in permitting this amount to pass, but in saying this now I should like to point out to the Government, as I had occasion to do this afternoon when another item was under consideration, that this must not he regarded as a precedent for future years. Something was said, when the first advance was asked for, about there being precedents in these matters. Well. Sir, it has developed now from precedent into habit on the part of the Government to ask for these advances, and this is due largely to the fact that Parliament is called so late in the year. I was speaking a few minutes ago with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) as to the reason why the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier fixed the fiscal year as it did, and my hon. friend assures me that I was right when I said this afternoon that it was to enable Parliament to meet in November rather than away on in January or February. It gave time to the Auditor General to audit the accounts necessary for the Auditor General's Report, and the departments time to prepare their estimates. When Parliament met in November and proceeded with its business with despatch, the items required for public busines could for the most part be passed before we reached the end of the fiscal year. I want to say, not by way of threat but simply that hon. gentlemen opposite will understand the position of the Opposition, that if the Government of the day should by any possibility be in office next year we shall not be willing to make these advances. We shall expect the Government to call Parliament earlier than was done this year and to have public business sufficiently under way to enable the due control to be exercised over public expenditures which Parliament ought to have.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I can very -well appreciate the motives of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) hut I am very much afraid that the reasons he has given will not convince the Government, because I do not believe that they are open to conviction. I have discussed this matter with quite a number of gentlemen on both sides of the House and without exception they ail express the opinion that it is simply ridiculous to begin the session of Parliament towards spring and keep members here until the month of July. Yet the Government persists in this course, and they are so obdurate that I am afraid the leader of the Opposition has only spoken in vain in attempting to convert them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I am a new hand; I might be easily converted.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext:
Well, so far as the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) is concerned the remarks of my leader may prove effective. But I know that the other ministers do not take this representation seriously. They are not here to please hon. members but rather to do as they see fit and call upon their supporters, whether those gentlemen agree with them or not, to support them upon the floor of the House. But I challenge any one to deny that ninety per cent of the members on the other side of the House are not satisfied with the course which the Government obstinately pursues in calling Parliament together when it does. Every hon. member believes that it is wrong and unfair to call the session at such a time that the House is kept sitting till July. Some members have to leave for their fields and others have to attend to their various businesses. 'Is there any reason why the session should not begin early in January? I see no reason at all why it should not. Sir Wilfrid Laurier used to call the session in the month of November, and he was wise in doing so, notwithstanding the fact that he was criticised for bringing members to Ottawa a few weeks before the New Year instead of after. There is no reason in the world why Parliament should not convene between the 10th and 15th January each year. We quite . understand that after the last general election, on account of the fact that the returns had to be brought from overseas under the law which was then in force, we had to wait until March. Consequently the Government were not to blame for beginning the session in March, 1918; it was the force of circumstances. But in the following year they had no reason to begin late. Last

year there was no reason to begin the session as late as it was begun and close it on the 7th of July. This year there was no reason again for calling the session so late. We are going into the month of July very soon. It is not fair to hon. members that the Government should use their strength to adopt such a procedure against the will of ninety per cent at least of members of the House.

I am quite sure my hon. friend does not want to do anything that is unreasonable. I am also quite sure that he is aware that I cannot give any promise that will bind anybody. I am at one with my hon. friend in wishing for a more expeditious conduct of the business of the House and for a shorter session. Anything I can do that will shorten the session without in any way jeopardizing that full and free discussion and consideration which the different subjects we have to deal with demands, I shall be only too glad to do. After all, the great thing is to get our business through. I regret just as much as the hon. member the length of the time we think it necessary to remain here.

I am not blaming anybody, I am not excusing any one, I am simply saying that it is unfortunate that we have to again ask for another supplementary vote. The fact is we have done a good deal of work, although we have done some talking, too.. I entirely agree with my hon. friend that we should have shorter sessions and that members should be able to get away at an earlier date.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-THE INTERIM SUPPLY BILL.
speechtext: I am not rising to oppose the motion, I will give my consent to it in a moment; but I want it to be well understood that my objection was not to the length of the session; the minister misunderstands me altogether. I said the session should be called earlier in the year, not later than January, and on this point I asked for an answer. No one but the Government is responsible. I know that the minister is acting in good faith and I excuse him from responsibility from the position we are in, but surely if the Government want to make some promise they can, without endangering their position, make some promise and say that next year the session will begin not later than the month of January.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

1.	Resolved, That towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty, on account of certain expenses of the Public Service for the financial year ending 31st March, 1920, the sum of $3,175,199.81 be granted out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
2.	Resolved, That towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty, on account of certain expenses of the Public Service for the financial year ending 31st March, 1921, the sum of $64,984,319.42' be granted out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
Resolutions agreed to.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

Sir HENRY DRAYTON thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 166 for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the Public Service for the fiscal years ending 31st March, 1920, and 31st March,
1921.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the first and second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time, and passed.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Sir HENRY DRAYTON moved that the House do again go into Committee of Supply.
Hon. W. . L. MACKENZIE KING (Prince): Does not my hon. friend think we have covered sufficient ground to-day? We have certainly voted a good deal of money.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have waited a long time for this happy moment, and I would not like it to pass now. If we can go into Supply and deal with the Soldiers' Land Settlement Estimates-which have already been before the House on two previous occasions, once for half a day and this afternoon for an hour-I will not ask the House to sit longer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the item?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. 275.
Motion agreed to and the House went again into Committee of Supply, Mr. Steele in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When the committee adjourned at six o'clock the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) asked for certain particulars as to the fees paid to law firms in Ontario. I had explained that in Ontario the old system still prevailed of employing a firm of solicitors to report on titles, paying them according to a scale of fees fixed1 by the Department of Justice. The firm engaged in Ontario was Messrs. Jones and Leonard, and1 the total fees per title in respect of mortgages averaged about $14; in respect to purchases of land and subsequent loans thereon the fees averaged $31.70. I realize that on something over
1,000	loans the total is a very considerable sum, although it extends over a period of a couple of years. Nevertheless, Messrs. Jones & Leonard have on more than one occasion asked to be relieved of the work, claiming that it has not paid them to act for the board, and it has been only at the urgent request of the board that they have consented to continue. We hope, however,
[Sir Henry Drayton.!
to install in Ontario the same system as we have in force in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick and, I think, in Nova Scotia,-a system of departmental legal branches, by means of which we have got through our legal work at an expense approximating less than a quarter of what it has cost us under the old system.
Does the soldier or the Government pay that fee?
Do those figures contain the disbursements to the Registry Office and so forth? *

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. In the first class of cases the disbursements are about $7 extra, and in t'he latter class of cases a little over $9 extra. The Government pays all the fees in respect to the search of title for the soldier.

In regard to the amendment introduced to the Soldiers' Settlement Act, which was given its first reading on the I5th of April, according to the old Act the soldier settlers did not make any payment on interest or capital account on their stock and equipment loans until the end of the third year. Do I understand that under the amendment they will now pay interest from the date of their loans?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hoard has power to exact that from the soldier settler who settles on improved land; but as respects the settler who brings new land under cultivation, he gets at least the equal of the two years, and a further concession in that his whole loan can be deferred for an extra year and no collection made upon it. That special advantage is given to the man who settles on unimproved land. But the board can, since the passage of the amendment, exact from the settler on improved land interest from the beginning, that is to say, there is no final remission of interest at all as respects that man, and though the board do not collect the interest at first, ultimately he may be called upon to pay the whole of it.
Will this be retroactive and apply to soldiers who have already been settled by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not at all.

I suppose this is a suitable time for me to ask the minister what the views of the Government are with regard to the re-establishment of returned soldiers who are fishermen. The question was raised by me last year

and I think that some rather favourable expression of opinion was given by a member of the Government, but nothing has been done. In Eastern Canada especially a large number of our soldiers were recruited from followers of the fishing industry. When these men returned-

This
question would be more appropriate if put when the Estimates of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment were under consideration. We are now considering the matter of soldiers' land settlement.

I think I can get an answer from the Government at this time, if the minister will permit me. It is well known that these men have not been given very much encouragement in the way of re-establishment. It does not take a great deal of money to re-establish a fisherman. I am told by men who are familiar with the expenditure required that something in the vicinity of $2,000 or $2,500 would be sufficient to equip a fisherman with a boat and all the nets and gear that he requires for his (business. These men are not suited to farm work; they cannot take advantage of the land settlement proposals; their business is on the sea. The fishermen are a very important part of our population in Eastern Canada, and I think that some consideration ought to be given to them. They turned out to be just as good soldiers as the men who wentjfrom the farms, and they should not be deprived of the advantage of assistance simply because they are fishermen and not farmers. Every reason that exists for re-establishing a farmer on the land exists for re-establishing a fisherman on the sea. They are both producers; they are equally important to the future of the country; and the Government should take just as much interest in the one class as in the other. True, fishermen are not so numerous as the fanners, but man to man [DOT]they are just as important. I would like to know what the views of the minister and of the Government are on this question. I am quite certain that the Government have considered the matter. '

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no question as to the merits of the fishermen who are returned soldiers and as to the desirability of assisting them to re-establish themselves ini their calling, if any practical means can be devised. So far the Government have launched upon a loaning system applicable only to those engaged in agricultural pursuits. That is not because those seeking to engage in agriculture
[Mr. Sinclair.j
are more deserving from the standpoint of the soldier than those seeking to engage in mechanics, or in fisheries, or in any other honourable pursuit; it is merely because a more practical method can be devised for assisting the first class than the latter; because more tangible and permanent security is obtained, better machinery is available and, as is generally admitted, agriculture is our basic industry. It may be pretty strongly argued that fisheries come next or very close to the next to agriculture, and that if any further branching out could be done it might well be in that direction. Consequently we have seen to it that the question of the admission of those desiring to go into fishing to the benefits of the soldier settlement scheme should be very carefully reviewed. I understand that the matter is now before the pensions and re-establishment committee of this House; that they have been and are receiving evidence and hearing the best opinion that can be heard on the subject. As that is the case and as the Government before deciding would like to hear their judgment in the matter, after full inquiry, I would not care to make any definite comitment at the present time. I would like to add this, though: that the board, though sympathetic toward the request of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) who has urged upon us and upon the board the desirability of this venture, is naturally reluctant to go further at the present time, unless, of course, the demands in the public interest are overwhelming. The pressure upon the board for assistance in agriculture has been so great and is at the present moment at so high a point that they would not like to have the numbers multiplied any more than they can avoid. They are finding it difficult indeed properly to guard the public interest and keep their organization at such a degree of efficiency as will take care of so extreme and urgent a demand as now bears upon them and have regard at the same time to conserving the treasury of the country and the ultimate public interest when amounts so huge are involved. Nevertheless the Government awaits the report of that committee; we feel that Parliament cannot with advantage discuss the subject while that report is still outstanding.

I am
glad to know that the Government has an open mind on the question and that there is a chance of something being done. The minister is doubtful about the security the fishermen could give. I quite agree that the security of land is more stable; as some

old legal authority has said: "You cannot run away with an acre of land." That is. true, but if you insure a fisherman's boat and provide him with the necessary gear, the investment is a pretty safe one-safer, in my opinion than an investment on the security of an old, run-out farm. If the soldier fails on a country faTm and cannot make a living on it, the farm is impoverished, and in that respect the security in many parts of Canada is not very good. You would find quicker sale in the Maritime Provinces for a fisherman's boat, if it was kept in good order and insured against accident, than you would for such a farm as I have mentioned. Moreover, the fisherman can begin to produce much quicker than the farmer. Suppose you give a fisherman a boat to-day. The summer fishing is on now. The mackerel will be here in shoals in a few weeks; the haddock will come in November. The fisherman can begin to pay back in six months, if he is successful, as he would likely be in many cases. The farmer takes a couple of years to contribute anything at all, so that the returns would come much more quickly in the case of the fishermen, and with proper care and insurance there would not be much more risk than there is in the case of the farmer.

Is it not the case that
most of the fishermen in the Maritime Provinces still receive every spring a subsidy under the old Washington Treaty to help them with their equipment and nets? Does the hon. member wish to give them something in addition to that?

The
subsidy is not worth talking about; it is a mere trifle, and it belongs to the fishermen themselves. It does not come from the Government. The history of the subsidy is that many years ago a lawsuit was brought by the Dominion of Canada against the United States for treepassing on the inshore fisheries of the Maritime Provinces. I think the award given was $3,000,000, although I am not sure as to the amount. At all events this amount was placed to the credit of the fishing industry and the interest of that money which was secured to the fishermen by the lawsuit is paid in bounties each year. A fisherman with an ordinary fishing boat receives only between three and four dollars a year. The amount is not worth talking about, and besides it is theif own money.

What has this to do
with land settlement?
[iMr. Sinclair.]

I think
the committee will make better progress if we confine the discussion to the resolution before the committee.
How many men are employed by the board for administration in the district of Sherbrooke?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Eighteen.
And in Quebec city?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Eleven.
How many loans were made in the district of Sherbrooke?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The total number in
Quebec is 362; in the district of Sherbrooke, 297, and in Quebec city, 65.
Will the minister kindly give the same information for district No. 6, Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There were 319 for
Halifax up to the 27th March last.

How many men has
the minister employed in district No. 6?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Twenty-two.

Does the minister not think that this staff could be reduced? My im. pression-and I say this not by way of criticism, but as a suggestion-is that the staff employed by the board in almost every city is too large and could be reduced without any loss of efficiency. ' I am informed, for instance, that in the district of Sherbrooke, eighteen men are employed who, for the eighteen months that they have been in service, have had to deal with 297 loans. The staff seems to be very large for such little business, and the same statement applies to a large number of other districts.
Another matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is this. In many instances the vendor of a property has made an agreement with the prospective purchaser by which the value has been enhanced so as to allow the soldier not to make any payment on account and even to make a profit by the transaction. I have been advised from a most reliable source that when a farm was offered for $5,000, the soldier had to pay 10 joer cent on $5,000, but he would go to the owner of the farm and say:	"Ask $6,000." In this way the
Government would advance $5,400 although the real purchase was only $5,000. In many instances speculation of that kind has occurred. I do not know what steps the Government could take to avoid that, but the

Government could surely find some way out of the difficulty in the future, and at the same time, they should reduce the staff in many districts.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are at the present
time reducing the staff in the province of Quebec, and particularly in Quebec city. The amount of business in Quebec city does not warrant a continuation on the present scale, and we are reducing the status of that office to the rank of an ordinary supervision office, wre are not making it a regular Soldier Settlement centre. As regards Sherbrooke, that cannot be done; there is considerable business at Sherbrooke, and such business as there is requires very close supervision. The staff has to deal not only with the 297 men who are settled, but with applications from many more. Just at the present time the 'number is higher than it will average generally, and a little later on the number will be reduced. We do not go in for keeping any staff beyond the absolute necessities of the time, and I do not think there can be found in any part of Canada a staff where the employees are not working on their tiptoes. That may he, perhaps, too strong as regards all the offices, but I do not think an office can be found where at least very satisfactory work is not being performed by all the staff.
As regards the hon. member's report that soldiers, in order to avoid the 10 per cent payment, have induced vendors to raise their prices, and, I presume, to give the soldiers fake receipts for the initial payments, thereby relieving them of that obligation, the Soldier Settlement Board and myself will be only too glad if the hon. member will furnish us with a single instance where that has been done. I am not saying this by way of challenge or by way of intimation that there has been no such case. When a board is dealing with 36,000 to 50,000 people, and is purchasing and lending money on 20,000 separate farms in every constituency in Canada, it would be only fatuous to contend that there could be no case where the ingenuity of the individual had not managed to beat out the board. I do not think there are many such cases.
Is there a sworn statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We get statements
from every vendor. We make him tell us where he got the land, when he got it, what he paid for it, and he has to certify to the terms at which he is selling and to the bona fides of it. In any case where there is a complaint-there is one at the present
time. It has been heard before the Reestablishment Committee. We had in that very case an investigation going on before we had any report from any outside party at all. We had in that case, as we have in every case, a certificate from the man as to what he paid for the land and when he got it. I may say that in this particular case the vendor has managed to escape. I will consider it a service on the part of the hon. member if he will just give me a description of the land and the namte of the vendor in any case where a soldier has managed, or is reported to have managed to have got the best of the board in such a manner as that or in any other manner, and I will give him my undertaking that it will be traced to the bottom and fitting steps will be taken to right the matter. I may say that in every case where I have endeavoured to get to details I have not always been successful. They have usually remained between heaven and earth and have not been made known to the board.

What is the total number
of officers and men on the staff of the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: 1,321. On the 27th of March last the number was 1,321. It is 'about the same to-day.

That does not
agree with the statement made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). Discussing this question on the 1st of June, in accounting for the very large increase that had been made in the Civil Service, he said:
There has been an increase of 1,257 in the Soldiers' Settlement Board, and it was absolutely essential that that board should be manned to carry on its important work. Does anybody question that? Then there were 6,296 appointed in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Estab-Kshment, which is so essential for the re-establishment of our soldiers in civil life; and 275 on the staff of the Board of Pension Commissioners. Thus there was an aggregate increase in those four departments of 8,48'5.
Those figures are much largeT than the figures given by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are smaller. The President of the Privy Council gave 1,257 as the number added to the Soldiers' Settlement Board. The total number I gave was 1,321.
That is an increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is an increase because the whole board has been created since that time mentioned by the hon.

member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair.) I must commend the President of the Privy Council for his usual accuracy in giving those figures.
Hoav many travelling inspectors are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There are 190 on the
staff of supervisors.

What becomes of free
grants of land made by Provincial Governments? For instance, in the province of Quebec, and I presume in the province of Ontario, soldiers are allowed to take out 100 or 160 acres from the Provincial Government. Are they in any way helped by the Soldier Settlement Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh yes, just the same as any other soldier settler. As soon as he has a proposition that appeals to the board as one that he can pay for, and at the same time make a living upon, whether he got the land by way of grant from a Provincial Government or in any other way, the board is ready to assist him just the same as any other settler. That principle applies as to Provincial Government assistance in every province of Canada.

But the title to these
lands obtained from the Provincial Governments is not vested in the soldier until he has fulfilled certain conditions, a residence of five years and certain payments, and so forth. Just what stand does the board take with reference to these cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course, under our
Act we cannot assist any soldier by way of loan until we get a first mortgage on the lands. I understand that in the province of Quebec arrangements have not been come to yet by which the province agrees to turn over the title of the land to the board. Until they do that we cannot under our Act give any assistance to the soldier on that land, but just as soon as they will do it we are not only ready but anxious to assist the soldier on that land the same as on any other. But we annot do it until they turn over the title.

Suppose the soldier wants to settle on land in Abitibi, Metapedia, or any other part of the province. The province has already remitted the dues in the case of the soldier, which the ordinary settler has to pay. Of course, you cannot expect the province to say: We will give you a free grant of land. The soldier must fulfil certain conditions with regard to residence and duties. I think the minister and

the department ought to be able to evolve some scheme whereby these men who have obtained help from the Department of Colonization of the province could receive assistance from the board. That is true colonization, because the man is taking up new land. It is not like the settlement we are getting from the board now, where a poor farmer buys out a good one. Here is a man who wants to establish himself on the land and clear it in true pioneer fashion. This is the man we should help, but apparently we are not able to do so. Cannot the minister evolve a scheme for assisting that man?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The minister has succeeded in evolving a scheme, but the Government of the province of Quebec has not succeeded in acquiescing.
What is the minister's scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the province of British Columbia, where the resources are owned by the province, the same question arises. After considerable difficulty we managed to make an arrangement, an arrangement that we are quite ready to make along similar lines with the province of Quebec, whereby the province turns the title of these grants, which they make subject to settlement duty, over to the board in order that the board may have the security which the Soldier Settlement Act compels it to have before it can give assistance; and the province leaves to the board the determination of the completion of the settlement duties. There is no other way in which it can be done. The Government of British Columbia has now acquiesced, I am informed, and we are therefore able to go ahead and give assistance to settlers on provincial homestead lands in that province. We will be only too glad to do the same in the province of Quebec, and I appeal to my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) to use his well-known vast influence with the Government of that province to bring them to the viewpoint of the Government of British Columbia, so that we can do for the soldiers of Quebec the same as we do for the soldiers of British Columbia.

In order to use this influence I would like the minister to explain a little more fully. Suppose the soldier in the province of Quebec goes away at the end of two years, whereas the conditions require, say, a five-year settlement. I understand that the title to the land would then be vested in the Dominion, that the land would become Crown land.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
To the extent of our
claim, but I understand the province has the right to pay off the claim of the Dominion and have the land revert to the province.
That is hardly likely, because in no case would these lands be worth the amount which the board was willing to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh yes, because our money has gone into the land.

But the province would
hardly pay that money back to the Dominion. They have so much land that they want to settle that they would not pay $1,500 or $2,000 or $3,000 to get that land back.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What does the hon. member think we should do? Lose the money?
Suppose the province refuses to pay the money, what happens?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have the land.
It is vested in the Crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
How many men defaulted last year on the conditions^of their contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Only 1.71 per cent of
the number of farmers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When this item was up before, the minister took occasion to say that there was no foundation for the charges made by the Great War Veterans' Association of Canada with reference to the administration of the Soldiers' Settlement Act, and in that connection he made what has been interpreted as an attack upon one of the officers of the Dominion Executive. There has been a good deal of comment in the press upon what was said by the minister at the time in reference to this officer, and I wondered whether the minister had anything to say in regard to the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The minister, being a lawyer, has such respect for cases that are sub judice that he would not venture to make further comment on it at the present time.
What salaries are paid the supervisors?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: From $1,500 to $2,400 according to grade. We have assistant supervisors and chief supervisors. The latter, who are the best and most experienced, go up to $2,400.
And expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Has the board arrived at any decision with reference to the disposal of the Stewart farm near Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a farm that has to do with the Civil Ee-establishment Department; we do not own it.
I was under the impression that the Land Settlement Department was training men on that farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not correct.

Has anything been done to enable the returned men to take up irrigated land in Alberta? The minister will remember that on the occasion of his visit to southern' Alberta last year representations were made that assistance should be provided for soldiers to 'settle on irrigated land. And he will also remember that the Canadian Pacific railway had established a colony for soldiers on their irrigated section in southern Alberta, and it was meeting with success. I shall be glad if the minister will make a statement on the subjedt.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am glad to say that we have decided to go as far as, if indeed not further, than I intimated on the occasion of that visit. I was indeed impressed by visiting the irrigated farms of Alberta with the possibilities of farming there, and it appeared to me as wholly unjustifiable that we should adopt iany entirely negative attitude toward irrigated land, even though the prices were much in excess of ordinary land. We are prepared to assist, in accordance with the provisions of the Soldier Settlement Act, men who desire to settle upon irrigated land or upon irrigable land, on one condition, and that is certainty as to water supply. Just as soon as the board is satisfied, not that there is water available at the moment but that a [DOT]water supply is certain, and that the property is not merely an irrigable one but that provision is already made to 'bring a sure water supply to it, then we are ready to take the band of the soldier and help him settle on that land and afford him the assistance of the Soldier Settlement Act.	,

Has any suggestion been made to the board that those undergoing training in agriculture should have their salaries or wages increased to the same amount as paid soldiers undergoing vocational training?

.1224

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; we do not contemplate that. These are physically fit men whoi after training .are probably going to get something more substantial in the way of assistance from the State, and consequently we do not think that their scale of allowances should be as high as that which is accorded to disabled men who, after they undergo a period of training, do not receive this substantial assistance. We think that the present scale is fairly reasonable under the circumstances.
Is the present scale based on the cost of living?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It has relation to the cost of living.
Is it supposed to be sufficient to keep a man and his family during the period of training?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not supposed to do that.

The man must have means of his own?
Mr. ME'IGHEN: No, but he must have energy of his own. For example, a single man who is put out to training, who is informed that he must go and learn farming, being hired with a farmer, does not get any assistance. He gets the help that the farmer gives him; he is supposed to earn his way when he is learning to be a fanner. The married man who is doing the same work gets $20 a month, and $6 for the first child and $5 for the others, not exceeding a certain total of, I think, $25. The married man gets that by way of supplementary assistance. Those receiving training in institutions get board and free training. The married men get $35 per month, $6 for the first child and $5 for each subsequent child. The single man gets $10 a month.
What is the length of the training period?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We give a man three months. He does not get training in higher agriculture. He is simply taught the rudiments of farming, so that he may be some good when he gets on land. The agricultural college is intended to make a good farmer a better farmer, and the course of training that is given to the man who is put on the farm is intended to make a green farmer a real farmer. As to the man who works for a farmer in order to learn agriculture, he is usually given a month first at one of these training centres in order that he may be of some use when he is on

the land. After he spends his time on the land, usually nearly a year, he is then given his finishing course of two months; so that he gets a course of three months in all.
Resolutions reported.
On motion of Rt. Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 12 midnight.
Tuesday, June 8, 1920.
